To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

patients place importance on not rushing during bad news consultations, the doctors manner, the doctor being the best judge of information needs, the doctor being a good communicator and being able to adapt, the doctor being able to personalize their approach, the doctor being empathetic and the doctor being able, and willing, to talk about the emotional impact of the diagnosis.
patients with haematologic cancer want to receive bad news from their doctor, who should be the best judge of what and how to tell them, in a manner that is unhurried, empathetic and personalized.

patients with haematologic cancer want the following from their doctors when they receive bad news: to be listened to; not to be rushed; to be given time to absorb and ask questions; to be told what to expect; to be told about the likely emotional impact of diagnosis; to be told who will be their main point of contact; to be given written information; and to have a companion present.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to improve the process of breaking bad news to patients with haematology cancer.
the experience of receiving a diagnosis of haematological cancer.
the process and content, not just the delivery, of bad news.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
patients with haematologic malignancy want the bad news delivered in a way that is personal, compassionate, and tailored to their individual needs and circumstances.
the patients’ experience of receiving bad news is important to them and that the way in which this is done is important to them.

patients with a diagnosis or suspected diagnosis of leukaemias or lymphomas, who were interviewed in a haematological outpatient department, had a range of preferences and needs in relation to the process and content when receiving bad news.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the patient is a person, not a case.
the patients we interviewed were very satisfied with the way they had been told about their illness, and the information and support they had received.
we should not only be aware of the guidelines but also be able to understand the patient’s perspective.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the patient is a key partner in the BBN process and that their perspective is a vital part of the BBN process.
patients with haematologic malignancies are very concerned about the process and content with which their doctors communicate bad news.
patients want doctors to be their guide and support on a journey of uncertainty and fear.
